slides.title: Groups Become Geometry
slides.notes: Open by naming the central move of the chapter: a group is not drawn directly. We choose generators, build a Cayley graph, measure word distance, and then ask which large-scale patterns survive better choices. Keep the slide grounded in the source span so students see this as the course doorway, not a detached survey.

slides.title: The Geometric Group Theory Loop
slides.notes: Use the loop as the working contract for the whole course. Algebra supplies elements, generators, and relations; geometry supplies a graph and a metric; coarse invariants translate the picture back into algebraic information. Emphasize that every arrow is a choice that must be checked, not a decorative slogan.

slides.title: Cayley Graph Rule
slides.notes: Define the Cayley graph operationally. For each group element g and generator s, draw an edge from g to gs. When the generating set is symmetric the drawing can be treated as undirected, but the multiplication rule is still the engine. The local star around g is the whole construction repeated everywhere.

slides.title: Word Metric
slides.notes: Present word length as the distance from the identity in the Cayley graph. A word is a route, and the metric asks for the shortest route after using all relations. This is the first moment where algebraic simplification and graph distance become the same kind of evidence.

slides.title: Three First Models
slides.notes: Compare the three finite windows without pretending they exhaust the infinite groups. The line for Z has two large directions, the grid for Z squared spreads across a plane, and the free group branches without cycles. Ask students to ignore boundary artifacts and inspect the pattern near the identity.

slides.title: Relations Fold Geometry
slides.notes: The free group begins as a tree because reduced words do not close up. Adding a relation identifies different words, and those identifications fold the tree into cycles or grids. The commutation relation ab equals ba is the cleanest first fold because it turns two routes into the same endpoint.

slides.title: Generator Choices Are Local Choices
slides.notes: Stress that a Cayley graph depends on a generating set, but geometric group theory is interested in patterns robust under reasonable generator changes. For Z, adding a two-step generator creates shortcut edges and changes small distances, yet the large object still looks line-like at coarse scale.

slides.title: Coarse Questions Preview The Course
slides.notes: The opening chapter does not prove the later invariants, but it prepares their questions. Growth asks how balls expand, ends ask how many directions remain after removing a large core, hyperbolicity asks whether triangles are thin, and amenability asks whether boundary can be small compared with volume.

slides.title: Worked Metric Checks
slides.notes: Make the metric concrete with two quick checks. In the standard grid, the shortest route from the identity to (3,2) has length five. In a free group, adjacent inverse letters cancel before length is read. These examples show why the graph metric remembers relations without storing a multiplication table on the slide.

slides.title: Finite Windows Are Evidence
slides.notes: Finite Cayley graph balls are microscope views of an infinite object. They are useful only when the inspection target is stable as the window grows. Boundary vertices are artifacts of the cutoff, while branching, cycles, approximate growth, and recurring distance envelopes are meaningful signals.

slides.title: Lab Move: Add One Relation
slides.notes: Frame the lab as a prediction exercise before computation. Start with the free tree, add a single relation, and say what should happen geometrically. A torsion relation should close a cycle; a commutation relation should create squares; a longer relation should fold branches along a repeating path.

slides.title: Chapter 01 Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the loop. Cayley graphs provide the first bridge from algebra to metric geometry, word metrics turn multiplication into distance, and coarse questions deliberately ignore finite local noise. The students should leave able to explain why groups can be studied as spaces.
